document_summary:
The survey frames the current bottleneck in industrial robotics as a control problem that demands rapid commissioning, safe human proximity, and flexible adaptation to varied tasks, environments, and sensing modalities. To meet these needs the authors propose **Robotic Foundation Models (RFMs)**—large‑scale, self‑supervised systems that ingest multimodal inputs (proprioception, exteroception, language) and generate diverse outputs ranging from high‑level plans to low‑level commands. RFMs are positioned within a five‑level hierarchy of control, with Vision‑Language‑Action (VLA) models highlighted as a key sub‑category that fuses vision and language into a shared token space, enabling end‑to‑end training and human‑like instructability. The authors distinguish single‑purpose RFMs (e.g., perception‑only) from general‑purpose RFMs that remain embodiment‑independent, supporting manipulation, locomotion, aerial, underwater and hybrid mobile‑manipulation robots.

A systematic literature pipeline translates user‑provided ASQS queries into native searches across arXiv, Google Scholar, OpenAlex, Scopus and Semantic Scholar, merges results, de‑duplicates, enriches metadata and applies GPT‑4o‑based relevance filtering. The **main corpus** comprises 1 025 papers, of which 341 describe control‑oriented RFMs (324 manipulation‑focused). An **industrial‑implication corpus** of 125 manually vetted papers supplies requirements, while auxiliary searches add 113 further works. This process yields a reproducible, transparent dataset.

From the industrial‑implication corpus the authors derive **eleven inter‑dependent implications** (adaptability, safety/compliance, HRI, robustness, precision, real‑time performance, cost‑effectiveness, explainability, sensor fusion, benchmarking, data requirements). These are expanded into 47 concrete attributes and a 149‑item criteria catalogue covering model capabilities, ecosystem documentation, and joint logging/usability concerns. Redundancy is intentional to allow fine‑grained diagnosis of immaturity in specific dimensions.

The hardware survey of 180 articulated cobots (average 6 DOF, payload 8.6 kg, reach ≈ 970 mm, accuracy ≈ 0.09 mm, power ≈ 0.31 kW) details sensor suites (RGB/D, LiDAR, TOF, IMU, force/torque) and edge compute options. NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano offers the best price‑performance for low‑latency inference; higher‑end Orin AGX, Thor and RTX 5090 provide greater throughput at substantially higher power and operating cost, with industrial‑grade variants adding ECC memory and further expense.

An automated evaluation pipeline uses GPT‑5.1 to assess each of the 324 manipulation‑capable RFMs against every criterion (48 276 decisions). The system is conservative: ambiguous evidence yields a “unfulfilled” label, producing lower‑bound maturity estimates. Validation against three expert‑rated papers shows 96.6 % accuracy, 1.9 % false‑positives and 22.6 % false‑negatives, the latter mainly due to vague criterion definitions.

Results reveal uniformly low maturity: most models score below 0.04, a few reach ≈ 0.2, and the top outlier (Gemini Robotics 1.5) attains 0.12 total (0.44 on adaptability alone). Per‑criterion maxima are modest (0.31 for generalisation, 0.29 for safety/robustness). Adaptability, benchmarking and data efficiency are the only implications with near‑full coverage; safety, HRI, real‑time performance and cost‑effectiveness remain largely absent (average coverage < 0.07). Only ~19 % meet any explainability‑trust benchmark, <10 % expose perceptual features, and privacy or confidence‑score reporting is missing.

The authors conclude that current RFMs are fragmented, excelling in isolated dimensions while lacking integrated, industry‑grade capabilities. They call for co‑design of models and edge hardware, stronger safety and reliability guarantees, richer benchmarking that includes distribution‑shift robustness and long‑horizon operation, and systematic logging and governance. The 149‑item catalogue is presented as a living framework to guide future research toward auditable, production‑ready robotic intelligence. Limitations include unrecoverable table data (marked 「結構未能可靠重建」) and reliance on LLM‑based annotation without external validation, which may bias the reported scores.
